# Laparoscopic surgery

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Abdominal surgery > General abdominal surgery > Laparoscopic surgery*

[Original Article Link](/library/B50zmg)

---

## Summary

Laparoscopic <u>surgery</u> is a minimally invasive technique used to perform surgical procedures within the <u>abdominal cavity</u>, utilizing specialized instruments introduced through small <u>incisions</u> made on the abdominal wall. The <u>abdominal cavity</u> is first accessed using a <u>trocar</u> or a <u>Veress needle</u>, most commonly in the midline (peri-umbilical region). The <u>peritoneal cavity</u> is then insufflated with carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>). A fiber-optic instrument (laparoscope) is inserted into the first <u>trocar</u> to visualize the <u>abdominal cavity</u> and to allow for other ports to be created under direct <u>vision</u>. Laparoscopy is often the preferred diagnostic procedure for most elective gastrointestinal and gynecological surgeries. It is contraindicated in patients with <u>shock</u>, cardiac/pulmonary failure, and in cases of dilated bowel loops/perforation <u>peritonitis</u>. There are several advantages of laparoscopy over <u>laparotomy</u> as the <u>incisions</u> used are much smaller (e.g., less postoperative <u>pain</u>, fewer respiratory complications). However, the <u>surgery</u> is technically more challenging and complications (e.g., hemorrhage, bowel injury) are difficult to control laparoscopically. Complications unique to laparoscopy (secondary to CO<sub>2</sub> insufflation of the <u>peritoneal cavity</u>) include <u>hypercarbia</u>, <u>pneumothorax</u>, <u>pneumomediastinum</u>, <u>venous air embolism</u>, and postoperative shoulder <u>pain</u>. Proper patient selection and good surgical technique minimize the risks and complications of laparoscopy.

---

## Indications

Nearly all elective abdominopelvic surgeries can be performed laparoscopically. A few examples include:




* Gastrointestinal <u>surgery</u>: : e.g., <u>cholecystectomy</u>, <u>appendectomy</u>, <u>hernia</u> repair, <u>bowel resection</u>

* Gynecological <u>surgery</u>: : e.g., <u>hysterectomy</u>, <u>oophorectomy</u>

* Urological <u>surgery</u>: e.g., <u>nephrectomy</u>, pyeloplasty

* Diagnostic laparoscopy

* Allows direct visualization of the <u>abdominal cavity</u>, as well as <u>biopsy</u> of suspicious areas (<u>lymphadenopathy</u>) or collection of <u>peritoneal</u> fluid (for culture or <u>cytology</u>) through small <u>incisions</u> in the abdominal wall. [[1]](/library/x4aElk)

* Commonly used to avoid <u>laparotomy</u> in the following situations:

* Evaluation of <u>acute abdominal pain</u> with negative imaging

* Abdominal trauma with negative imaging when an intra-abdominal injury is suspected (e.g., <u>diaphragmatic tear</u>)

* Staging of cancers

* To determine resectability of cancers: <u>gastric cancer</u>, <u>pancreatic</u>/<u>biliary tract cancer</u>, etc.

---

## Contraindications

* <u>Absolute contraindications</u> [[2]](/library/A4aRNk)

* <u>Hemodynamic instability</u>/<u>shock</u>

* Acute <u>intestinal obstruction</u> with dilated bowel loops

* <u>Increased intracranial pressure</u>

* <u>Relative contraindications</u> [[2]](/library/A4aRNk)[[3]](/library/-4aDNk)

* Cardiac failure

* Pulmonary failure

* <u>Pregnancy</u>/large <u>pelvic</u> masses

* <u>Soft tissue infection</u> at port sites

* Expected (extensive) adhesions from a previous abdominal <u>surgery</u>

* <u>Abdominal aortic aneurysm</u> (may be associated with increased risk of vascular rupture)




We list the most important contraindications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Advantages and disadvantages of laparoscopy

* Advantages of laparoscopy over <u>laparotomy</u> include:

* Less postoperative <u>pain</u>, which leads to:

* Early mobilization → decreased risk of developing <u>deep vein thrombosis</u>, <u>pulmonary embolism</u>, or <u>pneumonia</u>

* Minimal use of <u>analgesics</u>

* Shorter hospital stay

* Shorter duration of <u>postoperative ileus</u>

* Better cosmetic outcome (smaller scars)

* Less intra-abdominal adhesion formation

* Disadvantages of laparoscopy are mainly technical:

* The surgical field is converted to a two-dimensional image on a monitor.

* Technically more challenging than <u>laparotomy</u>

* Difficulty in controlling intra-operative hemorrhage

* Laparoscopy-specific complications (see below)

---

## Complications

### Intra-operative complications




* Injury to adjacent organs (e.g., <u>blood vessels</u>, bowel, <u>bladder</u>, solid intra-abdominal organs)

* Injury to structures adjacent to <u>surgery</u> site (e.g., <u>blood vessels</u>, bowel, <u>bladder</u>, solid intraabdominal organs)
* Bowel injury [[7]](/library/_cW5U40)[[8]](/library/zcWrU40)

* A rare but potentially life-threatening complication that may occur at any step of the <u>surgery</u>

* Intraoperative signs of <u>bowel perforation</u>

* Foul-smelling gas

* Leakage of bowel contents

* High insufflation pressure

* Asymmetric abdomen distention

* Symptoms of <u>bowel perforation</u> (e.g., <u>abdominal guarding</u>, absent <u>bowel sounds</u>, <u>signs of peritonitis</u>) may not develop until later in the postoperative period.

* <u>Aspiration</u> of gastric contents

* Intra-abdominal pressures > 20 mmHg should be avoided as it may potentially lead to:

* The <u>diaphragm</u> being pushed upwards → decreased total <u>lung</u> volume and increased <u>airway</u> pressure

* Compression of the <u>IVC</u> → decreased <u>venous return</u> to the <u>heart</u> → decreased <u>cardiac output</u>

* Increased <u>systemic vascular resistance</u> (compression of <u>arteries</u>) and release of <u>catecholamines</u> (<u>adrenaline</u>, <u>noradrenaline</u>) → <u>tachycardia</u>

* Compression of <u>renal arteries</u> → decreased <u>glomerular filtration rate</u> → decreased urine output

* <u>Pneumothorax</u>  [[9]](/library/7ka46k)

* <u>Pneumomediastinum</u> (rare)  [[10]](/library/HkaK6k)

* Subcutaneous emphysema  [[11]](/library/GkaB6k)

* Condition that results from entrapment of air or gas into the subcutaneous tissues

* Typically presents with sudden, painless <u>soft tissue</u> swelling, often around the upper chest, neck, and face

* <u>Hypercarbia</u> and <u>respiratory acidosis</u>

* <u>Venous air embolism</u> (rare)  [[12]](/library/tkaXpk)





> [!NOTE]
> Most intra-operative complications (<u>pneumothorax</u>, <u>respiratory acidosis</u>, <u>air embolism</u>) are indications to convert the procedure to a <u>laparotomy</u> (open procedure).




### <u>Postoperative complications</u>




* Early <u>postoperative complications</u> [[13]](/library/Fkagpk)

* Shoulder <u>pain</u>

* <u>Atelectasis</u>

* <u>Deep vein thrombosis</u>

* Late <u>postoperative complications</u>

* <u>Incisional hernia</u>

* Port site <u>metastasis</u>





We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
